feedback.message: So close! Did you skip one? Point at each star as you say a number word.
Nearly! Maybe one star got two number words. Touch each star only once.

hints: Point at the first star and say *one*. Move to the next star and say *two*.
Keep going until every star has had exactly one word. The last word you say is the answer.
exercises.solution: Touching each star once: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight. The last word is *eight*, so there are **8** stars.

exercises.prompt: All of Nomin's goats have gone out to the grassland. How many goats are left in the pen?

feedback.message: There is one *pen*, but how many goats are inside it?
Seven goats went *out*. How many are still *in* the pen?

hints: If every goat has gone out, is there anything left in the pen to count?
When there is nothing to count, the number is zero.
exercises.solution: The pen is empty, so there are **0** goats in it. Zero is the number of members of the empty collection.

exercises.prompt: Kofi counts his marbles: *one, two, three, four, five, six*. He says *six* just as he touches the blue marble. How many marbles does Kofi have?

options.label: 6 marbles
options.feedback: Yes! The last word Kofi said tells how many marbles there are altogether.

options.label: Only the blue marble is *six*
options.feedback: The blue marble is not called *six*. The last word tells how many marbles there are in the **whole** collection.

options.label: We can't tell without counting again
options.feedback: If Kofi counted carefully, his last word already tells us. Counting again in any order would give *six* again.

hints: What does the last number word tell us when we count?
Does *six* belong to one marble, or to the whole collection?
exercises.solution: When we count carefully, the **last** number word tells how many things there are. Kofi's last word was *six*, so he has **6** marbles.

exercises.prompt: Lina puts 5 buttons in a short row: 🔵🔵🔵🔵🔵. Mei puts 5 buttons in a long row: 🔴  🔴  🔴  🔴  🔴. Who has more buttons?

options.label: Lina
options.feedback: Lina's buttons are closer together. Does that make more of them? Try pairing each of Lina's buttons with one of Mei's.

options.label: Mei, because her row is longer
options.feedback: A longer row is not always more. Pair each of Mei's buttons with one of Lina's — is any button left over?

options.label: They have the same number
options.feedback: Yes! Each of Mei's buttons can be paired with one of Lina's, with none left over. Spreading out does not make more.

hints: Count each row. What is the last word you say for each one?
Or pair the buttons: one of Lina's with one of Mei's. Is any button left without a partner?
exercises.solution: Both rows end on *five* when you count them, and the buttons pair up with none left over. So they have **the same number**. Mei's row is longer only because her buttons are spread out.

exercises.prompt: Six children sit down for lunch: 🧒🧒🧒🧒🧒🧒. There are five plates: 🍽️🍽️🍽️🍽️🍽️. Each child takes one plate. What happens?

options.label: One child has no plate
options.feedback: Yes! When we pair children with plates, one child is left over. There are fewer plates than children.

options.label: One plate is left over
options.feedback: Pair them up: one child with one plate. Which runs out first — the children or the plates?

options.label: Every child gets exactly one plate, with none left over
options.feedback: That would happen only if there were the same number of children and plates. Try pairing them.

hints: Match the first child with the first plate, the second child with the second plate, and so on.
When the plates run out, is there still a child waiting?
exercises.solution: Pairing children with plates uses up all 5 plates, and 1 child is left without one. So **one child has no plate**: 5 is less than 6. We found this out by pairing, without needing to count.

exercises.prompt: Amara counted the goats standing in a ring and got 10. But there are really 9 goats. What mistake might she have made?

options.label: She counted the first goat again when she came back round
options.feedback: Yes! In a ring it is easy to count your starting goat twice. Marking where you started helps.

options.label: She skipped a goat
options.feedback: Skipping a goat would give a number that is too *small*. Amara's answer was too big.

options.label: The goats were spread out, so there were more
options.feedback: Spreading out never changes how many goats there are. Amara's count went wrong somewhere.

hints: Is 10 too big or too small?
In a ring there is no end. How do you know when to stop counting?
exercises.solution: Her answer was one too many, so one goat got two number words. In a ring, the usual slip is to count the first goat again when you come back round to it. Marking the starting goat, or moving each goat as you count it, prevents this.

exercises.prompt: Sticks are tied in bundles of ten. There are **6 bundles** and **3 loose sticks**. How many sticks are there altogether?

feedback.message: 6 + 3 counts the bundles as if each were one stick. But each bundle has **ten** sticks in it!
Careful with the order: the bundles are tens and the loose sticks are ones. Count the bundles first: ten, twenty, …

hints: Count the bundles in tens: ten, twenty, thirty, …
Six bundles make sixty. Now count on the 3 loose sticks: sixty-one, …
exercises.solution: Count the bundles in tens: ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, **sixty**. Then count on the loose sticks: sixty-one, sixty-two, **sixty-three**. There are **63** sticks.

feedback.message: 98 comes just *before* 99. Which number comes just after it?
After 9 tens and 9 ones comes 9 tens and 10 ones — and 10 ones make another ten. How many tens is that?

hints: 99 is nine tens and nine ones. Add one more one.
Ten ones make a ten, and ten tens make one hundred.
exercises.solution: One more than 99 is **100**. Nine tens and nine ones, plus one more one, make nine tens and ten ones; the ten ones make another ten, and ten tens make **one hundred**.

exercises.prompt: Gideon's game: is this statement true or false? *"There is a biggest counting number."*

options.label: True — a million is the biggest
options.feedback: A million is big! But what about a million and one?

options.label: False — every number has a next one
options.feedback: Yes! Whatever number someone says, one more is bigger. So no number can be the biggest.

hints: Think of a very big number. Can you say a bigger one?
What happens if you add one?
exercises.solution: The statement is **false**. Whatever number you choose, the next number (one more) is bigger, so no number is the biggest. Gideon only needed one argument that works for *every* number — he did not have to check them all.

exercises.prompt: Margaret's computer counted 5 goats in every possible order — 120 different orders. In how many of those 120 orders was the last number word *five*?

feedback.message: Only one order? Think: does changing the order change how many goats there are?
Every order touches all 5 goats once. What is the last word each time?
24 is the number of orders for 4 goats. Here every one of the 120 orders counts all 5 goats.

hints: Does counting in a different order add or take away any goats?
If every order ends on *five*, how many of the 120 orders end on *five*?
exercises.solution: In **all 120** orders the last word was *five*. Changing the order changes which goat gets which word, but every goat still gets exactly one word, so the count always ends on *five*. Margaret's computer checked this herd; the explanation in the lesson shows why it is true for every collection.
